newsitem.title: UK: Funds see APEC trade meet aiding Asia investment.
newsitem.headline: Funds see APEC trade meet aiding Asia investment.

text.p: Global investors expect next week's meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to lead to a free-trade zone which should help the region fight off growing competition from Latin America and Eastern Europe.
The APEC summit starting on Monday in Manila brings together 18 countries with the goal of axing trade barriers by 2020.

The group comprises Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.

"The APEC meeting reinforces leaders' commitment to free trade in a region where exports are already very important," said JP Morgan ASEAN economist Vincent Low. "In the last few years, the key has been trade, liberalisation and investment."
That is likely to draw investors. But Regent Fund Management's Sophia Shaw said less competitive Asian economies could soon find themselves elbowed out by growing competition from other regions.

"I think some of the more closed Asian markets are going to have to try hard to compete for foreign investment, and they're not only competing with amongst each other but also with Latin America and eastern Europe," Shaw said.
ANZ Grindlays economist Chris Portman agreed that other markets would challenge Asia's position as the world's preferred high-yield investment destination.

"Latin America will pose increasingly strong competition to Asian countries as economic growth there is accelerating," Portman said. "Eastern Europe would generally be considered lower risk than most Asian emerging markets."
But many fund managers say part of the attraction of Asia is its volatile markets which offer higher returns.

JP Morgan economist Jan Loeys said rapid economic growth had fuelled speculative interest in Asia. "Speculators have become disappointed with trading opportunities in many major markets because there is not enough volatility," Loeys said.
"And so they're moving out to emerging markets because they traditionally think there are not many knowledgeable players there and it is "easy' to make money."
Loeys said he saw strong demand for Asian high-yielding assets which also provide investors with portfolio diversity.
"Many major asset markets have become more and more correlated, and the investor who is looking for diversification must look towards developing countries," he said.
"There is a strong demand from asset managers for playing the currency markets in Asia, because currency volatility in a lot of other markets has been collapsing."

Fleming Investment Management Pacific region analyst Peter Warwick said the firm was overweight Asia in general, particularly Hong Kong, Indonesia and India but was underweight Korea, Taiwan and Thailand.

One fund manager said Korean short term bond yields could help the equity market in the short term. "But structural problems within the economy, and in particular the corporate sector, continue to justify a bear stance in the market."

Warwick said Korean electronics were on the verge of recovering from a slump, semiconductor prices were about to start rising and the market would benefit from signals that the yen was not appreciating.

"In Thailand, on the other hand, there's big talk of a devaluation of the baht, and they're raising rates when the economy is slowing down," Warwick said. India and Indonesia were extremely cheap markets, he added.

Warwick said Asian exports were bound to expand next year as economic growth in its markets picked up. "The APEC move is going to strengthen Asia. If you're going to lower barriers, it automatically makes you more competitive," he added.
